solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Purveyor of indulgences settled in Tudor widow’s embrace (8)

indicatorNotes.embrace: the widow's name wraps its arms around the other piece

blocks.note: Catherine Parr, Henry VIII's last wife, who outlived him
a deal that is done is settled

annotation.surface: Some historical figure snug in the arms of Henry VIII's widow while selling pardons.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tudor widow' means the widow of a Tudor king: Henry VIII left only one. Chaucer's Pardoner is the best-known seller of indulgences.
annotation.definitionFit: A pardoner was a cleric licensed to sell papal indulgences.

entries.clue: He wrote two articles with 50 in abundant supply (1,1,5)

indicatorNotes.in: the 50 goes inside the word for abundant supply

annotation.surface: A description of a prolific writer, articles and figures piling up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'He wrote' is a slim definition: any writer would do, and the crossings decide it. 'Abundant supply' sounds like plenty; a mine is a rich source.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by bare description: Milne is a man who wrote, the author of Winnie-the-Pooh.

entries.clue: VIPs understand stars supporting fool (11)

indicatorNotes.supporting: in a down clue the stars sit below the fool, holding it up

annotation.surface: Important people are told to grasp that the celebrities are propping up an idiot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stars' pulls toward celebrities, and VIPs next to it strengthens that; here it is a star sign.
annotation.definitionFit: Dignitaries are very important persons.

entries.clue: Recalled Charlie wearing coat and trousers (5)

annotation.definitionNote: 'trousers' is a verb here: pockets, steals

indicatorNotes.Recalled: called back, so the coat is read in reverse
indicatorNotes.wearing: Charlie is inside, wearing the coat

blocks.note: an animal's coat is its skin

annotation.surface: Charlie has been summoned back, dressed in coat and trousers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' looks like clothing next to 'coat', but it is the verb to trouser, pocket money dishonestly; to nick is British for steal.
annotation.definitionFit: To trouser something is to pocket it, and to nick it is to steal it.

entries.clue: Debauchee gorging on roguish man’s dish (7)

indicatorNotes.gorging on: the debauchee swallows the man whole

blocks.note: a bit of a lad: a cheeky, roguish young man

annotation.surface: A rake stuffs himself with some rascal's food.
annotation.walkthrough: ROU(LAD)E. In British usage a 'lad' is a boisterous young man, which is why 'roguish' belongs to him.
annotation.definitionFit: A roulade is a rolled dish, meat or sponge rolled round a filling.

entries.clue: Julius Caesar — reluctant dish washer? (1-5)

annotation.surface: Caesar, mighty conqueror, drags his feet over the washing-up.
annotation.walkthrough: A J-cloth is a British brand of disposable cleaning cloth; the question mark admits that a cloth is only a dish washer by a stretch.
annotation.definitionFit: A J-cloth is used to wash dishes.

entries.clue: Name twice claimed by unidentified male poet (4,5)

indicatorNotes.claimed by: the two Ns are taken into the unidentified man's name

blocks.note: John Doe, the placeholder name for an unknown man

annotation.surface: An anonymous poet whose name gets claimed by two people.
annotation.walkthrough: JOHN DO(NN)E. John Doe is the American legal name for an unidentified man.
annotation.definitionFit: John Donne was a seventeenth-century English metaphysical poet.

entries.clue: Asian destination not good for climbing (3)

indicatorNotes.not: the letter for good is taken away
indicatorNotes.for climbing: in a down clue it reads upward

blocks.note: your goal is where you are heading

annotation.surface: A trekking destination in Asia said to be no good for climbing.
annotation.walkthrough: GOAL without G is OAL, which reads LAO going up. 'Climbing' plays on mountains, but it only turns the word.
annotation.definitionFit: Lao names the people and language of Laos, in South-East Asia, so it works as the noun or adjective Asian.

entries.clue: Fried food, possibly upmarket, lacking in potassium (7)

indicatorNotes.possibly: the letters might be arranged some other way
indicatorNotes.lacking in: something lacking in an ingredient has gone without it, so the K comes out

blocks.note: anagram fodder once K is gone

annotation.surface: A menu note about battered food that might be posh but lacks potassium.
annotation.walkthrough: UPMARKET without K leaves UPMARET, which rearranges to TEMPURA.
annotation.definitionFit: Tempura is Japanese battered and deep-fried food.

entries.clue: Something in meadow one might trip on? (5,8)

annotation.definition: Something in meadow one might trip on?

blocks.note: reads as a stone or tussock in the grass; it is something growing there
reads as stumble over; a trip is also a hallucinogenic experience, and one can be 'on' a drug

annotation.surface: A warning about something in the grass that could make a walker stumble.
annotation.walkthrough: You picture tripping over a tussock; the trip is a drug trip, and magic mushrooms grow wild in fields.
annotation.definitionFit: Magic mushrooms grow in meadows and cause hallucinogenic trips.

entries.clue: No tea for army clergy in open country (6)

indicatorNotes.No: the tea is dropped from the clergy

blocks.note: cha (char) is British slang for tea, removed

annotation.surface: Army chaplains out on the open plains go without their tea.
annotation.walkthrough: CHAPLAINS minus CHA leaves PLAINS.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: broad treeless flatland is what open country means.

entries.clue: Edmund died with a ruptured appendix (8)

indicatorNotes.ruptured: burst open, so the letters are broken up

annotation.surface: A death notice: Edmund died of a burst appendix.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface appendix is the organ; the definition is the kind added to the end of a book.
annotation.definitionFit: An addendum is material added at the end of a book, an appendix.

entries.clue: Is indebted to sport charges? Nothing about that in 2 book (3,2,3,3)

indicatorNotes.charges: OWES is loaded with WEAR, as a gun is charged

blocks.note: to sport a hat is to wear it

annotation.surface: A grumble about debts and sports fees, with nothing to say about them in the book.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Charges' reads as fees, but it is the verb: to charge is to load. The 2 is a cross-reference to 2 down, A. A. Milne.
annotation.definitionFit: Now We Are Six is A. A. Milne's 1927 book of children's verse.

entries.clue: Possible advice for dilatory chess player? (3,1,4,2)

annotation.definition: Possible advice for dilatory chess player?

blocks.note: the answer is a stock phrase someone might say
a slow player needs to hurry, and also literally to make a move on the board

annotation.surface: An opponent drumming their fingers at a slow chess player.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Get a move on' means hurry up, and for a chess player it is also the literal request to play a move.
annotation.definitionFit: Get a move on means hurry up, apt for someone slow to move at chess.

entries.clue: Supply has to operate outside old building (4,5)

indicatorNotes.Supply: read as the adverb of supple: bend these letters
indicatorNotes.outside: the pieces go round the letter for old

blocks.note: to use a machine is to operate it

annotation.surface: A demand that the supply chain be run from outside an old building.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a noun, but it is the adverb from supple, flexibly. An oast house is a kiln for drying hops, common in Kent.
annotation.definitionFit: An oast house is a building with a kiln for drying hops.

entries.clue: What used to make people blue without a lot of fuss? (4)

annotation.definition: What used to make people blue

indicatorNotes.a lot of: most of the word, not all of it

blocks.note: much ado; the last letter is dropped

annotation.surface: A wry question about what once made people blue without any bother.
annotation.walkthrough: W/O plus most of ADO. 'Blue' reads as sad, but the Ancient Britons painted themselves blue with woad.
annotation.definitionFit: Woad is a plant dye the ancient Britons used to paint their skin blue.

entries.clue: Julie’s content consuming gram in fruit (4)

indicatorNotes.content: only what is inside Julie, her outer letters gone
indicatorNotes.consuming: the inner letters swallow the gram

blocks.note: JULIE without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: Julie is happy eating a gram of fruit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Content' reads as happy; here it means contents. U(G)LI.
annotation.definitionFit: The ugli is a Jamaican citrus fruit, a tangelo.

entries.clue: Trouble afoot seemingly reduced desire for work (7)

indicatorNotes.reduced: the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: gout typically strikes the foot; the last letter is dropped

annotation.surface: Someone's foot trouble has sapped their appetite for work.
annotation.walkthrough: GOUT cut to GOU, then ACHE. 'Seemingly' concedes that 'trouble afoot' is a playful description of gout. 'Work' is a work of art.
annotation.definitionFit: A gouache is a painting in opaque watercolour, a work of art.

entries.clue: 14lb chicken Gabrielle gutted for rock group (10)

indicatorNotes.gutted: the insides of Gabrielle are removed

blocks.note: only the outer letters of GABRIELLE

annotation.surface: A heavy chicken that Gabrielle cleaned for a band.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rock group' wants to be a band; it is a group of standing stones on Salisbury Plain.
annotation.definitionFit: Stonehenge is a prehistoric circle of standing stones, a group of rocks.

entries.clue: Very large agricultural tool cutting middle of ankle bone (7)

indicatorNotes.cutting: the middle of ankle is cut from the tool

blocks.note: the centre letter of ANKLE, removed

annotation.surface: A huge farm implement slicing through the middle of an ankle bone.
annotation.walkthrough: OS plus SICKLE without K. 'Ankle bone' reads as the definition; the definition is 'bone' alone, and 'ankle' feeds the K.
annotation.definitionFit: An ossicle is a small bone, such as those in the middle ear.

entries.clue: Babushka topping it with a Sicilian dessert (7)

indicatorNotes.topping: in a down clue the grandmother sits on top

annotation.surface: A Russian grandmother garnishing a Sicilian sweet.
annotation.walkthrough: The Russian doll sense of babushka is a tease; it is the grandmother.
annotation.definitionFit: Granita is a Sicilian semi-frozen dessert of flavoured ice.

entries.clue: Subversive attempts holding Henry with new suspect (8)

indicatorNotes.new: the letters of suspect are made new

blocks.note: h = henry, the unit of inductance

annotation.surface: Plotters holding a man called Henry alongside a fresh suspect.
annotation.walkthrough: PUTSC(H)ES. 'Suspect' looks like a noun in the plot, but it is the letters to be rearranged.
annotation.definitionFit: A putsch is an attempted coup, a subversive attempt to seize power.

entries.clue: Opening in harbour exposed wall (6)

annotation.surface: A gap in a harbour's exposed sea wall.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Exposed' looks like a description of the wall; it strips the wall bare to AL.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a portal is a grand doorway, an opening in a wall.

entries.clue: City district with church, without hotel (5)

indicatorNotes.without: a district without a hotel lacks one, so the H is taken out of the word

blocks.note: a parish is the area served by a church

annotation.surface: A travel note on a city district with a church but no hotel.
annotation.walkthrough: PARISH minus H.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Paris, capital of France, is one example of a city.

entries.clue: Busy arresting King: US novelist heard in college (6,7)

indicatorNotes.arresting: the policeman holds the king, as a cop would
indicatorNotes.heard: the novelist's name is spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: a busy is British slang for a police officer

annotation.surface: A police officer nabs Stephen King, the American novelist, overheard at a college.
annotation.walkthrough: 'King: US novelist' paints Stephen King, but King is just R inside CO(R)P, and the novelist is Agatha Christie.
annotation.definitionFit: Corpus Christi is a college at both Oxford and Cambridge.

entries.clue: Uncovered real meaning in boring routine (3)

blocks.note: the truth is what is really meant

annotation.surface: Someone discovers the real point hidden in a dull routine.
annotation.walkthrough: TRUTH without its covers leaves RUT. 'Uncovered' reads as found out, but it takes off the edges.
annotation.definitionFit: Figurative: a wheel stuck in a groove in the road became the image for a monotonous habit.

entries.clue: Labour politician perhaps in story broken by English paper (6)

indicatorNotes.broken by: the story is split open to let the other pieces in

annotation.surface: A Labour MP's story gets overturned by an English newspaper.
annotation.walkthrough: L(E FT)IE. Labour is the UK's main left-of-centre party; 'perhaps' because not every Labour politician is a leftie.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by 'perhaps': Labour sits on the left, so its members are often called lefties.

entries.clue: Brash individual somehow means to pen classical number (5,3)

indicatorNotes.somehow: the letters of means are rearranged somehow
indicatorNotes.to pen: they enclose the number, as a pen holds sheep

annotation.surface: Some loudmouth intends to write a piece of classical music.
annotation.walkthrough: ES(SEX)MAN. 'Classical number' sounds musical but is Latin. Essex Man is the British stereotype of a brash, newly affluent voter from Essex, the county east of London.
annotation.definitionFit: Essex man is a stereotype of a brash, materialistic, working-class man.
